claim: The insect central complex (CX) is thought to underlie goal-oriented navigation.
source: The insect central complex (CX) is thought to underlie goal-oriented navigation but its functional organization is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established scientific understanding about the CX.

claim: The functional organization of the insect central complex is not fully understood.
source: The insect central complex (CX) is thought to underlie goal-oriented navigation but its functional organization is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract acknowledging a gap in current understanding.

claim: A group of neurons targeting the ventral fan-shaped body (ventral P-FNs) are robustly tuned for airflow direction.
source: We found that a group of neurons targeting the ventral fan-shaped body (ventral P-FNs) are robustly tuned for airflow direction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on recordings from genetically-identified neurons.

claim: Ventral P-FNs did not generate a 'map' of airflow direction.
source: Ventral P-FNs did not generate a 'map' of airflow direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on analysis of neuronal responses across different columns.

claim: Cells in each hemisphere of ventral P-FNs were tuned to 45° ipsilateral, forming a pair of orthogonal bases.
source: Instead, cells in each hemisphere were tuned to 45° ipsilateral, forming a pair of orthogonal bases.
evidence: This is a finding from the study describing the organization of airflow tuning in ventral P-FNs.

claim: Ventral P-FNs inherit their airflow tuning from neurons that provide input from the lateral accessory lobe (LAL) to the noduli (NO).
source: Imaging experiments suggest that ventral P-FNs inherit their airflow tuning from neurons that provide input from the lateral accessory lobe (LAL) to the noduli (NO).
evidence: This is a conclusion from imaging experiments presented in the study.

claim: Silencing ventral P-FNs prevented flies from selecting appropriate corrective turns following changes in airflow direction.
source: Silencing ventral P-FNs prevented flies from selecting appropriate corrective turns following changes in airflow direction.
evidence: This is a finding from genetic silencing experiments in a flight simulator.

claim: Ventral P-FNs are required for proper orientation to airflow stimulus.
source: Our results identify a group of CX neurons that robustly encode airflow direction and are required for proper orientation to this stimulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on silencing experiments.

claim: Many animals compare and combine visual, mechanosensory and olfactory cues to achieve their navigational goals.
source: Many animals are known to compare and combine visual, mechanosensory and olfactory cues to achieve their navigational goals (Gire et al., 2016; Holland et al., 2009; Bianco and Engert, 2015; Dacke et al., 2019; Cardé and Willis, 2008; Lockery, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The central complex is a conserved brain region in insects.
source: In insects, a conserved brain region known as the central complex (CX) is thought to control many aspects of navigation (Strauss and Heisenberg, 1993; Honkanen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The central complex is thought to control many aspects of navigation in insects.
source: In insects, a conserved brain region known as the central complex (CX) is thought to control many aspects of navigation (Strauss and Heisenberg, 1993; Honkanen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The CX is a highly organized neuropil consisting of four primary subregions: the protocerebral bridge (PB), the ellipsoid body (EB), the fan-shaped body (FB), and the paired noduli (NO).
source: The CX is a highly organized neuropil consisting of four primary subregions: the protocerebral bridge (PB), the ellipsoid body (EB), the fan-shaped body (FB), and the paired noduli (NO).
evidence: This is a description of CX anatomy based on established knowledge.

claim: Columnar neurons recurrently connect CX regions to each other.
source: Columnar neurons recurrently connect these regions to each other, while tangential neurons targeting different layers of the EB and FB provide a large number of inputs from the rest of the brain (Hanesch et al., 1989; Wolff et al., 2015; Franconville et al., 2018; Hulse et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Tangential neurons targeting different layers of the EB and FB provide a large number of inputs from the rest of the brain.
source: Columnar neurons recurrently connect these regions to each other, while tangential neurons targeting different layers of the EB and FB provide a large number of inputs from the rest of the brain (Hanesch et al., 1989; Wolff et al., 2015; Franconville et al., 2018; Hulse et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Outputs from the CX are provided by different subsets of columnar neurons.
source: Outputs are provided by different subsets of columnar neurons (Stone et al., 2017; Franconville et al., 2018; Scheffer et al., 2020; Hulse et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In the EB, a group of 'compass neurons' (or E-PGs) exhibit an abstract map of heading angle that is derived from both visual and airflow landmark cues.
source: In the EB, a group of 'compass neurons' (or E-PGs) exhibit an abstract map of heading angle that is derived from both visual and airflow landmark cues (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Green et al., 2017; Fisher et al., 2019; Shiozaki et al., 2020; Okubo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: P-ENs rotate the E-PG heading representation when the fly turns in darkness.
source: Another set of EB neurons, known as P-ENs, rotate this heading representation when the fly turns in darkness (Green et al., 2017; Turner-Evans et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The EB compass network is not required for all forms of goal-directed navigation.
source: Despite these robust representations of navigation-relevant variables, the EB compass network is not required for all forms of goal-directed navigation.
evidence: This statement is supported by subsequent citations to prior research.

claim: Silencing E-PGs disrupts menotaxis but not other kinds of visual orienting.
source: Silencing E-PGs disrupts menotaxis—straight-line navigation by keeping a visual landmark at an arbitrary angle—but not other kinds of visual orienting (Giraldo et al., 2018; Green et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cockroaches alter their climbing and turning strategies when the FB is lesioned.
source: For example, cockroaches alter their climbing and turning strategies when the FB is lesioned (Harley and Ritzmann, 2010), while FB stimulation evokes stereotypic walking maneuvers (Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: FB stimulation evokes stereotypic walking maneuvers.
source: For example, cockroaches alter their climbing and turning strategies when the FB is lesioned (Harley and Ritzmann, 2010), while FB stimulation evokes stereotypic walking maneuvers (Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 'Compass'-like signals encoding heading and steering are present in some parts of the FB.
source: However, 'compass'-like signals encoding heading and steering are also present in some parts of the FB (Shiozaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Columnar neurons of the FB have been proposed to represent a desired heading.
source: Columnar neurons of the FB have been proposed to represent a desired heading, while output neurons of the FB have been proposed to drive steering (Stone et al., 2017; Honkanen et al., 2019), but these hypotheses have not been directly tested experimentally.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research and notes the hypotheses have not been tested.

claim: Output neurons of the FB have been proposed to drive steering.
source: Columnar neurons of the FB have been proposed to represent a desired heading, while output neurons of the FB have been proposed to drive steering (Stone et al., 2017; Honkanen et al., 2019), but these hypotheses have not been directly tested experimentally.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research and notes the hypotheses have not been tested.

claim: How the FB participates in navigation, and whether its role is distinct from that of the EB, is currently unclear.
source: How the FB participates in navigation, and whether its role is distinct from that of the EB, is currently unclear.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging a gap in current understanding.

claim: FB neurons represent a wide array of sensory cues, including optic flow, polarized light, and mechanical activation of the antennae or halteres.
source: As in the EB, FB neurons represent a wide array of sensory cues, including optic flow, polarized light, and mechanical activation of the antennae or halteres (Weir and Dickinson, 2015; Heinze et al., 2009; Ritzmann et al., 2008; Phillips-Portillo, 2012; Kathman and Fox, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Flow of the air or water is a critical mechanosensory cue for animals navigating in aquatic, terrestrial, and air-borne environments.
source: Although it has received less attention than vision or olfaction, flow of the air or water is a critical mechanosensory cue for animals navigating in aquatic, terrestrial, and air-borne environments (Montgomery et al., 1997; Yu et al., 2016a; Alerstam et al., 2011; Reynolds et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The primary sensors that detect flow are well-described in many species.
source: The primary sensors that detect flow are well-described in many species (Suli et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2016b; Yorozu et al., 2009), but an understanding of the higher brain circuits that process flow signals is just beginning to emerge (Okubo et al., 2020; Suver et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: An understanding of the higher brain circuits that process flow signals is just beginning to emerge.
source: The primary sensors that detect flow are well-described in many species (Suli et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2016b; Yorozu et al., 2009), but an understanding of the higher brain circuits that process flow signals is just beginning to emerge (Okubo et al., 2020; Suver et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: The neurons and computations that directly support flow-based navigation remain unknown.
source: The neurons and computations that directly support flow-based navigation remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging a gap in current understanding.

claim: The study used whole-cell recordings to systematically investigate the sensory responses of many of the major columnar cell types in the CX in open loop.
source: Here, we used whole-cell recordings to systematically investigate the sensory responses of many of the major columnar cell types in the CX in open loop.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The study measured responses to three stimuli known to elicit basic orienting responses in Drosophila: a visual stripe, directional airflow, and an attractive odor.
source: We measured responses to three stimuli known to elicit basic orienting responses in Drosophila: a visual stripe, directional airflow, and an attractive odor.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli used in the study.

claim: The ventral P-FN category contains the PFNa, PFNm, and PFNp cell types identified in recent connectomics studies.
source: The ventral P-FN category contains the PFNa, PFNm, and PFNp cell types identified in recent connectomics studies (Scheffer et al., 2020; Hulse et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement links the cell types studied to those identified in connectomics studies.

claim: Recordings from different columns suggest that ventral P-FN sensory responses are not organized in a sensory 'compass' or 'map'.
source: Recordings from different columns suggest that ventral P-FN sensory responses are not organized in a sensory 'compass' or 'map'—where all possible stimulus directions are represented (Fisher et al., 2019; Okubo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on recordings from different columns.

claim: Ventral P-FNs primarily encode airflow arriving from two directions, approximately 45° to the right and left of the midline.
source: Instead, ventral P-FNs primarily encode airflow arriving from two directions, approximately 45° to the right and left of the midline.
evidence: This is a finding from the study describing the organization of airflow encoding.

claim: Single neuron tuning in ventral P-FNs depended on the hemisphere in which its cell body was located.
source: Single neuron tuning depended on the hemisphere in which its cell body was located, with each FB column innervated by both left- and right-preferring neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the study describing the organization of tuning in ventral P-FNs.

claim: Each FB column is innervated by both left- and right-preferring ventral P-FN neurons.
source: Single neuron tuning depended on the hemisphere in which its cell body was located, with each FB column innervated by both left- and right-preferring neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the study describing the organization of innervation in the FB.

claim: The airflow representation in ventral P-FNs may be inherited from the lateral accessory lobe (LAL), which projects to the third nodulus compartment (NO3) in each hemisphere.
source: Imaging and recording experiments suggest that this airflow representation may be inherited from the lateral accessory lobe (LAL), which projects to the third nodulus compartment (NO3) in each hemisphere.
evidence: This is a conclusion from imaging and recording experiments in the study.

claim: The anatomy of LAL projections to NO3 could explain why all ventral P-FNs in one hemisphere share the same sensory tuning.
source: This anatomy could explain why all ventral P-FNs in one hemisphere share the same sensory tuning.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical observations.

claim: Flies with silenced ventral P-FNs fail to make appropriate corrective turns in response to a change in airflow direction.
source: Flies with silenced ventral P-FNs fail to make appropriate corrective turns in response to a change in airflow direction, but respond normally to airflow pauses, arguing for a specific role in linking directional sensory input to corrective motor actions.
evidence: This is a finding from genetic silencing experiments in the study.

claim: Flies with silenced ventral P-FNs respond normally to airflow pauses.
source: Flies with silenced ventral P-FNs fail to make appropriate corrective turns in response to a change in airflow direction, but respond normally to airflow pauses, arguing for a specific role in linking directional sensory input to corrective motor actions.
evidence: This is a finding from genetic silencing experiments in the study.

claim: Ventral P-FNs have a specific role in linking directional sensory input to corrective motor actions.
source: Flies with silenced ventral P-FNs fail to make appropriate corrective turns in response to a change in airflow direction, but respond normally to airflow pauses, arguing for a specific role in linking directional sensory input to corrective motor actions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on silencing experiments.

claim: Different CX compartments represent sensory information in distinct formats.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that different CX compartments represent sensory information in distinct formats, and identify a neural locus in the ventral FB that promotes orientation to airflow.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the findings.

claim: The ventral FB is a neural locus that promotes orientation to airflow.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that different CX compartments represent sensory information in distinct formats, and identify a neural locus in the ventral FB that promotes orientation to airflow.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the findings.

claim: Airflow responses were generally larger than stripe responses across cell types in the survey.
source: We found that, although most neurons responded to each cue in some manner, airflow responses were generally larger than stripe responses across cell types in the survey.
evidence: This is a finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: P-F1N3 neurons exhibited large directionally tuned spiking responses during airflow presentation, but not stripe presentation.
source: In P-F1N3 neurons, for example, large directionally tuned spiking responses were observed during airflow presentation, but not stripe presentation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F1N3 neurons.

claim: The cross-fly mean airflow response was larger than the mean stripe response in all cell types except P-F3N2v and P-EN1.
source: However, the cross-fly mean airflow response was larger than the mean stripe response in all cell types except P-F3N2v and P-EN1.
evidence: This is a finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: The difference between airflow and stripe responses was significant for P-F1N3, P-F2N3, P-F3N2d, and P-EN2.
source: This difference was significant for half of the cell types surveyed: P-F1N3, P-F2N3, P-F3N2d, and P-EN2.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: The strength of sensory tuning tended to vary with raw response magnitude.
source: The strength of sensory tuning tended to vary with raw response magnitude, with robustly responsive cell types also showing the strongest directional preferences (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: Many of the neurons recorded were tuned for the direction of airflow.
source: As such, many of the neurons we recorded were tuned for the direction of airflow (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: Tuning strength in the visual condition was relatively weak across recorded cell types.
source: In contrast to this strong directional preference in the airflow condition, tuning strength in the visual condition was relatively weak across recorded cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: P-EN1 neurons displayed modest visual tuning.
source: However, visual tuning was not completely absent – for example, P-EN1 neurons displayed modest visual tuning, in agreement with previous results (Turner-Evans et al., 2017; Green et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-EN1 neurons, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recorded E-PGs showed directional tuning to the stripe.
source: Recorded E-PGs showed directional tuning to the stripe (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), indicating that our stimulus can evoke tuned visual responses.
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of E-PG neurons.

claim: Adding odor to the airflow stream had only mild effects on CX columnar neuron responses.
source: Adding odor to the airflow stream had only mild effects on CX columnar neuron responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: Odor slightly reduced the airflow responses of P-F1N3 and P-F2N3.
source: Odor slightly reduced the airflow responses of P-F1N3 and P-F2N3 (Figure 1G), although this difference was only significant for P-F1N3.
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F1N3 and P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: Some single cells showed increases or decreases in spiking activity in the odor condition.
source: Some single cells also showed increases or decreases in spiking activity in the odor condition (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of CX columnar neurons.

claim: Pairs of columnar cells innervating the same NO compartment share similar sensory responses.
source: Broadly, our survey suggested that pairs of columnar cells innervating the same NO compartment share similar sensory responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: 'Ventral P-FNs', which receive input in layer 3 of the NO and ventral FB layers, had large airflow responses, showed olfactory suppression, and preferred ipsilateral airflow.
source: In particular, 'ventral P-FNs', which receive input in layer 3 of the NO and ventral FB layers, had large airflow responses, showed olfactory suppression, and preferred ipsilateral airflow (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: 'Dorsal P-FNs', which receive input in layer 2 of the NO, displayed modest sensory responses and ipsilateral airflow tuning in most cases.
source: 'Dorsal P-FNs', which receive input in layer 2 of the NO, and 'P-ENs', which receive input in layer 1 of the NO, both displayed modest sensory responses and ipsilateral airflow tuning in most cases.
evidence: This is a finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: 'P-ENs', which receive input in layer 1 of the NO, displayed modest sensory responses and ipsilateral airflow tuning in most cases.
source: 'Dorsal P-FNs', which receive input in layer 2 of the NO, and 'P-ENs', which receive input in layer 1 of the NO, both displayed modest sensory responses and ipsilateral airflow tuning in most cases.
evidence: This is a finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: The 'CX extrinsic' columnar neurons recorded both preferred contralateral airflow.
source: In contrast, the 'CX extrinsic' columnar neurons we recorded, which target neuropils outside the CX, both preferred contralateral airflow.
evidence: This is a finding from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: Sensory responses in CX neurons vary according to their input neuropils.
source: Thus, our survey suggests that sensory responses in CX neurons vary according to their input neuropils.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the survey of CX columnar cell types.

claim: Multi-sensory responses are, on average, approximately equal to the sum of single modality responses in most CX cell types.
source: When we plotted these measures for each cell type, we found that most points fell on or near the diagonal, indicating that multi-sensory responses are, on average, approximately equal to the sum of single modality responses.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of multi-sensory integration in CX neurons.

claim: The trend of near-perfect summation was also true when all three modalities were presented simultaneously.
source: This trend of near-perfect summation was also true when all three modalities were presented simultaneously (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of multi-sensory integration in CX neurons.

claim: Poly-modal integration generally proceeds via a summation principle for the stimuli presented in the study.
source: These results suggest that poly-modal integration generally proceeds via a summation principle, at least for the stimuli presented here, which were always presented from the same direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from analysis of multi-sensory integration in CX neurons.

claim: P-EN2 neurons showed remarkably consistent summation.
source: P-EN2 neurons, for example, showed remarkably consistent summation.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of multi-sensory integration in P-EN2 neurons.

claim: Single neuron spiking responses to multi-sensory cues strongly resembled the responses to single modality cues across all P-EN2s.
source: Single neuron spiking responses to multi-sensory cues strongly resembled the responses to single modality cues across all P-EN2s (Figure 2C, top).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of multi-sensory integration in P-EN2 neurons.

claim: P-F3N2d neurons show much greater integration diversity than P-EN2 neurons.
source: In contrast, P-F3N2d neurons show much greater integration diversity.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of multi-sensory integration in P-F3N2d neurons.

claim: Some P-F3N2d cells displayed multi-sensory activity that was dominated by the stripe response, while others were dominated by the airflow response.
source: While some cells displayed multi-sensory activity that was dominated by the stripe response, others were dominated by the airflow response (Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of multi-sensory integration in P-F3N2d neurons.

claim: Summation appears to govern P-F3N2d integration on average, but individual neurons show an array of sensory integration strategies.
source: Thus, while summation appears to govern P-F3N2d integration on average, individual neurons show an array of sensory integration strategies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from analysis of multi-sensory integration in P-F3N2d neurons.

claim: The trend of summation on average, but diversity at the single cell level, was found for many of the surveyed cell types.
source: This trend of summation on average, but diversity at the single cell level, was found for many of the surveyed cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion from analysis of multi-sensory integration in CX neurons.

claim: CX neurons integrate multi-modal sensory cues with compartment-specific variability.
source: These results suggest that CX neurons integrate multi-modal sensory cues with compartment-specific variability.
evidence: This is a conclusion from analysis of multi-sensory integration in CX neurons.

claim: P-F2N3 neurons had resting membrane potentials between −30 and −25 mV.
source: These cells had resting membrane potentials between −30 and −25 mV, and input resistances around 3 GOhm (Fig. S1).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: P-F2N3 neurons had input resistances around 3 GOhm.
source: These cells had resting membrane potentials between −30 and −25 mV, and input resistances around 3 GOhm (Fig. S1).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: P-F2N3s showed strong spiking responses to single presentations of ipsilateral airflow.
source: P-F2N3s showed strong spiking responses to single presentations of ipsilateral airflow, and active inhibition followed by offset spiking during single presentations of contralateral airflow (Figure 3B&D).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: P-F2N3s showed active inhibition followed by offset spiking during single presentations of contralateral airflow.
source: P-F2N3s showed strong spiking responses to single presentations of ipsilateral airflow, and active inhibition followed by offset spiking during single presentations of contralateral airflow (Figure 3B&D).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: Spiking activity in response to ipsilateral and contralateral airflow was relatively consistent from trial to trial in P-F2N3 neurons.
source: Spiking activity in response to ipsilateral and contralateral airflow was relatively consistent from trial to trial, while frontal and rear airflow elicited more diverse responses relative to baseline on each trial (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: Frontal and rear airflow elicited more diverse responses relative to baseline on each trial in P-F2N3 neurons.
source: Spiking activity in response to ipsilateral and contralateral airflow was relatively consistent from trial to trial, while frontal and rear airflow elicited more diverse responses relative to baseline on each trial (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: P-F2N3 neurons showed graded membrane potential and spiking responses to airflow, but not to the stripe.
source: On average, P-F2N3 neurons showed graded membrane potential and spiking responses to airflow, but not to the stripe (Figure 3C&E).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: Mean tuning across the P-F2N3 population did not change when the stripe, odor, or both, were added to airflow.
source: We found that mean tuning across the population did not change when the stripe, odor, or both, were added to airflow.
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: Each P-F2N3 neuron showed a large airflow correlation coefficient and a small visual coefficient.
source: Each P-F2N3 neuron showed a large airflow correlation coefficient and a small visual coefficient (Figure 3G), indicative of multi-sensory responses that strongly resemble the airflow-only response.
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: P-F1N3 sensory activity was similar to P-F2N3, except for the olfactory suppression.
source: P-F1N3 sensory activity was similar, except for the olfactory suppression noted above (Figure 3H&I).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F1N3 neurons.

claim: Individual ventral P-FNs target one CX column.
source: Like many other columnar cell types, individual ventral P-FNs target one CX column, with cell bodies in each hemisphere collectively innervating the eight outer columns of the ipsilateral PB and all eight columns of the FB (Wolff et al., 2015; Hulse et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cell bodies in each hemisphere of ventral P-FNs collectively innervate the eight outer columns of the ipsilateral PB and all eight columns of the FB.
source: Like many other columnar cell types, individual ventral P-FNs target one CX column, with cell bodies in each hemisphere collectively innervating the eight outer columns of the ipsilateral PB and all eight columns of the FB (Wolff et al., 2015; Hulse et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: All left-hemisphere P-F2N3 neurons responded strongly to airflow presented from the front-left and were inhibited by airflow from the rear-right, regardless of the column they innervated.
source: Surprisingly, we found that all left-hemisphere P-F2N3 neurons responded strongly to airflow presented from the front-left (between 0° and 90°, ipsilateral) and were inhibited by airflow from the rear-right (between −90° and −180, contralateral), regardless of the column they innervated.
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons across different columns.

claim: One right-hemisphere P-F2N3 neuron was excited by airflow from the front-right and inhibited by airflow from the rear-left.
source: One right-hemisphere neuron was excited by airflow from the front-right and inhibited by airflow from the rear-left.
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of a right-hemisphere P-F2N3 neuron.

claim: All P-F2N3 neurons show a preference for airflow presented ipsi-frontal relative to the hemisphere of their cell bodies.
source: Thus, all P-F2N3 neurons show a preference for airflow presented ipsi-frontal relative to the hemisphere of their cell bodies (Figure 4D&E), with peak tuning around approximately 45° ipsilateral.
evidence: This is a conclusion from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons across different columns.

claim: P-F2N3 neurons have peak tuning around approximately 45° ipsilateral.
source: Thus, all P-F2N3 neurons show a preference for airflow presented ipsi-frontal relative to the hemisphere of their cell bodies (Figure 4D&E), with peak tuning around approximately 45° ipsilateral.
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons across different columns.

claim: The spiking response to frontal airflow was strongest in the ipsilateral-most column 1 of P-F2N3 neurons, and was weaker in more contralateral columns.
source: The spiking response to frontal airflow (0°) was strongest in the ipsilateral-most column 1, and was weaker in more contralateral columns (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons across different columns.

claim: Membrane potential responses to contralateral airflow varied by column in P-F2N3 neurons, with contralateral columns exhibiting the greatest inhibition relative to baseline.
source: Membrane potential responses to contralateral also airflow varied by column, with contralateral columns exhibiting the greatest inhibition relative to baseline (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons across different columns.

claim: P-F2N3 neurons showed temporally diverse airflow responses.
source: P-F2N3 neurons also showed temporally diverse airflow responses (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: Some P-F2N3 neurons showed sustained activity during the stimulus period, while others displayed only transient responses to airflow presentation.
source: Some neurons showed sustained activity during the stimulus period, while others displayed only transient responses to airflow presentation.
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons.

claim: Temporal responses in P-F2N3 neurons were not reliably organized by column.
source: Temporal responses were not reliably organized by column (Figure 4J,K) but might instead reflect different behavioral states of the animal.
evidence: This is a finding from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons across different columns.

claim: Temporal responses in P-F2N3 neurons might reflect different behavioral states of the animal.
source: Temporal responses were not reliably organized by column (Figure 4J,K) but might instead reflect different behavioral states of the animal.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that temporal responses were not organized by column.

claim: Ventral P-FNs respond primarily to airflow, and not to the other stimuli presented in the cue set.
source: These data support two conclusions. First, ventral P-FNs respond primarily to airflow, and not to the other stimuli presented in our cue set.
evidence: This is a conclusion from recordings of ventral P-FNs.

claim: Airflow tuning across P-F2N3 neurons is not organized as a map of airflow direction, but is instead clustered around two directions approximately 45° to the left and right of the fly midline.
source: Second, airflow tuning across P-F2N3 neurons is not organized as a map of airflow direction, but is instead clustered around two directions approximately 45° to the left and right of the fly midline.
evidence: This is a conclusion from recordings of P-F2N3 neurons across different columns.

claim: The organization of airflow tuning in P-F2N3 neurons is reminiscent of the organization of optic flow responses in TN neurons of the bee.
source: This is reminiscent of the organization of optic flow responses in TN neurons of the bee (Stone et al., 2017), which have been proposed to act as basis vectors for computing movement of the animal through space.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research on bee TN neurons.

claim: TN neurons of the bee have been proposed to act as basis vectors for computing movement of the animal through space.
source: This is reminiscent of the organization of optic flow responses in TN neurons of the bee (Stone et al., 2017), which have been proposed to act as basis vectors for computing movement of the animal through space.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Each FB column is innervated by ventral P-FNs with cell bodies in both hemispheres.
source: Since each FB column is innervated by ventral P-FNs with cell bodies in both hemispheres, each column receives two orthogonal airflow signals that could be used to construct tuning to a variety of airflow directions in downstream neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on anatomical observations.

claim: Each FB column receives two orthogonal airflow signals that could be used to construct tuning to a variety of airflow directions in downstream neurons.
source: Since each FB column is innervated by ventral P-FNs with cell bodies in both hemispheres, each column receives two orthogonal airflow signals that could be used to construct tuning to a variety of airflow directions in downstream neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the organization of airflow tuning in ventral P-FNs.

claim: Neurons sensitive to airflow direction have recently been identified in both the antler (ATL) and the lateral accessory lobe (LAL).
source: Neurons sensitive to airflow direction have recently been identified in both the antler (ATL, Suver et al., 2019), and the lateral accessory lobe (LAL, Okubo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: A group of ventral FB neurons (vFBNs) receive input in the antler and appear to be presynaptic to ventral PFNs.
source: Using trans-tango experiments, we found that a group of ventral FB neurons (vFBNs) receive input in the antler and appear to be presynaptic to ventral PFNs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from trans-tango experiments.

claim: P-F2N3 neurons receive prominent input from LNa neurons that receive input in the LAL and project to the third compartment of the NO.
source: The Drosophila hemibrain connectome (Scheffer et al., 2020) indicates that P-F2N3 neurons (PFNa in the hemibrain) receive prominent input from LNa neurons (LAL-NO(a) neurons, Wolff and Rubin, 2018) that receive input in the LAL and project to the third compartment of the NO.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to connectomics data.

claim: LNa neurons, but not vFBNs, possessed directionally tuned airflow responses.
source: We found that LNa neurons, but not vFBNs, possessed directionally tuned airflow responses (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from recordings and imaging experiments.

claim: LNa neuron activity was strongly modulated by wind direction but not by the presence of odor.
source: Like ventral P-FNs, LNa neuron activity was strongly modulated by wind direction but not by the presence of odor (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from imaging experiments of LNa neurons.

claim: All of the strongly airflow-tuned ventral P-FNs receive input in the third compartment of the NO in one hemisphere.
source: Since all of the strongly airflow-tuned ventral P-FNs receive input in the third compartment of the NO in one hemisphere, this finding could explain why all ventral P-FNs in one hemisphere share similar sensory tuning.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical observations.

claim: Right-hemisphere LNas are connected to left-hemisphere ventral P-FNs, and vice-versa.
source: Right-hemisphere LNas are connected to left-hemisphere ventral P-FNs, and vice-versa (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an anatomical observation.

claim: LNa tuning was inverted compared to synaptically connected ventral P-FNs.
source: When we specifically compared the tuning of LNa neurons to synaptically connected ventral P-FNs, we found that LNa tuning was inverted (Figure 5C), suggesting that LNa neurons are inhibitory.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing tuning of LNa neurons and ventral P-FNs.

claim: LNa neurons are inhibitory.
source: When we specifically compared the tuning of LNa neurons to synaptically connected ventral P-FNs, we found that LNa tuning was inverted (Figure 5C), suggesting that LNa neurons are inhibitory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inverted tuning of LNa neurons compared to ventral P-FNs.

claim: Tuned airflow responses in ventral P-FNs are likely inherited from airflow-sensitive populations in the LAL (WL-L neurons).
source: Together, these results suggest that tuned airflow responses in ventral P-FNs are likely inherited from airflow-sensitive populations in the LAL (WL-L neurons, Okubo et al., 2020), although silencing experiments will be required to directly test the contribution of LNa and WL-L neurons to ventral P-FN sensory tuning.
evidence: This is a conclusion from imaging and recording experiments, with a note that further experiments are needed.

claim: Silencing experiments will be required to directly test the contribution of LNa and WL-L neurons to ventral P-FN sensory tuning.
source: Together, these results suggest that tuned airflow responses in ventral P-FNs are likely inherited from airflow-sensitive populations in the LAL (WL-L neurons, Okubo et al., 2020), although silencing experiments will be required to directly test the contribution of LNa and WL-L neurons to ventral P-FN sensory tuning.
evidence: This is a statement about future experiments needed to test the hypothesis.

claim: Flies prefer to orient away from the source of flow in a closed-loop flight simulator.
source: In previous experiments, we observed that flies prefer to orient away from the source of flow (Currier and Nagel, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Control flies adopted stable orientations away from the airflow source in the flight simulator.
source: Consistent with our previous results, control flies adopted stable orientations away from the airflow source (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments in the flight simulator.

claim: When either type of ventral P-FN was silenced with Kir2.1, flies displayed partially impaired orientation ability.
source: When either type of ventral P-FN was silenced with Kir2.1, flies displayed partially impaired orientation ability (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Flies with either type of ventral P-FN silenced showed increased orienting toward the flow and reduced orientation stability compared to controls.
source: These groups showed increased orienting toward the flow (Figure 6E) and reduced orientation stability (Figure 6F) compared to controls, although both effects were moderate.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Silencing R44B10-GAL4 neurons with Kir2.1 produced a more severe phenotype than silencing either type of ventral P-FN alone.
source: Silencing R44B10-GAL4 neurons with Kir2.1 produced a more severe phenotype (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced R44B10-GAL4 neurons.

claim: Flies with R44B10-GAL4 neurons silenced showed less stable orientation to airflow compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, these flies showed less stable orientation to airflow (Figure 6D), spent significantly more time oriented toward the airflow source (Figure 6E), and had reduced fixation strength (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced R44B10-GAL4 neurons.

claim: Flies with R44B10-GAL4 neurons silenced spent significantly more time oriented toward the airflow source compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, these flies showed less stable orientation to airflow (Figure 6D), spent significantly more time oriented toward the airflow source (Figure 6E), and had reduced fixation strength (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced R44B10-GAL4 neurons.

claim: Flies with R44B10-GAL4 neurons silenced had reduced fixation strength compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, these flies showed less stable orientation to airflow (Figure 6D), spent significantly more time oriented toward the airflow source (Figure 6E), and had reduced fixation strength (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced R44B10-GAL4 neurons.

claim: Ventral P-FNs are required for normal orientation to airflow.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that ventral P-FNs are required for normal orientation to airflow.
evidence: This is a conclusion from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Silencing E-PGs did not disrupt orientation to airflow.
source: In contrast to our experiments with ventral P-FNs, we found that silencing E-PGs did not disrupt orientation to airflow (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced E-PGs.

claim: In flies with silenced E-PGs, both the time spent orienting toward the airflow, and orientation stability, were indistinguishable from controls.
source: In flies with silenced E-PGs, both the time spent orienting toward the airflow, and orientation stability, were indistinguishable from controls (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced E-PGs.

claim: In response to airflow pauses, control flies briefly turned toward the airflow source.
source: In response to airflow pauses, control flies briefly turned toward the airflow source (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with stimulus perturbations.

claim: When the airflow resumed after a pause, control flies once again turned away.
source: When the airflow resumed, flies once again turned away (see also Currier and Nagel, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with stimulus perturbations, supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Overall turning in response to airflow pauses remained unchanged when both types of ventral P-FN were silenced.
source: Overall turning in response to airflow pauses remained unchanged when both types of ventral P-FN were silenced (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Despite the abnormal orienting behavior shown by ventral P-FN-silenced flies, they are still able to detect airflow and determine its direction.
source: These results suggest that, despite the abnormal orienting behavior shown by ventral P-FN-silenced flies, they are still able to detect airflow and determine its direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Silencing ventral P-FNs did not change the distribution of wingbeat angle differences compared to control flies.
source: However, we found no differences between the distributions of wingbeat angle differences for control and silenced flies (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Silencing ventral P-FNs did not change the distribution of integrated turn angles following airflow direction slips.
source: Similarly, silencing ventral P-FNs did not change the distribution of integrated turn angles following airflow direction slips (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Silencing ventral P-FNs leaves both sensory and motor function intact.
source: Together with our airflow pause data, these results suggest that silencing ventral P-FNs leaves both sensory and motor function intact.
evidence: This is a conclusion from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Silencing ventral P-FNs dramatically impaired the selection of turns following airflow direction slips.
source: In contrast, silencing ventral P-FNs dramatically impaired the selection of turns following airflow direction slips.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: In response to slips, control flies generally made corrective turns in the direction opposite the slip.
source: In response to slips, control flies generally made corrective turns in the direction opposite the slip (Figure 7F, top).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with stimulus perturbations.

claim: For rightward slips, control flies made turns to left, and for leftward slips, turns to the right.
source: For rightward slips, control flies made turns to left, and for leftward slips, turns to the right.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with stimulus perturbations.

claim: The duration and magnitude of the slip response varied with slip duration in control flies.
source: The duration and magnitude of the slip response varied with slip duration in control flies, such that turns following long slips (Figure 7F, left) were larger than turns following short slips (Figure 7F, right).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with stimulus perturbations.

claim: Control flies' reactive turns corrected for 45% of the orientation change induced by long slips, and 90% of short slips.
source: On average, control flies' reactive turns corrected for 45% of the orientation change induced by long slips, and 90% of short slips (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with stimulus perturbations.

claim: Flies with both types of ventral P-FNs silenced showed no turning response, on average, to slips of any direction or duration.
source: Conversely, flies with both types of ventral P-FNs silenced (R44B10-Gal4>UAS-Kir2.1) showed no turning response, on average, to slips of any direction or duration (Figure 7F&G).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: When only one type of ventral P-FN was silenced, a smaller reduction in mean slip responses was observed.
source: When only one type of ventral P-FN was silenced, we observed a smaller reduction in mean slip responses.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Silencing E-PGs did not disrupt slip correction.
source: Silencing E-PGs did not disrupt slip correction (Figure 7F&G), as expected based on the orientation behavior.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced E-PGs.

claim: Ventral P-FNs may be specifically involved in generating an appropriate turning response following a change in the direction of airflow.
source: Together, these results suggest that ventral P-FNs may be specifically involved in generating an appropriate turning response following a change in the direction of airflow.
evidence: This is a conclusion from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: The same sensory cue may be represented in different formats in different CX compartments.
source: A striking finding of our study is that the same sensory cue may be represented in different formats in different CX compartments (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the findings.

claim: A recent study found a map-like representation of wind direction in E-PGs, with different directions systematically represented across columns.
source: For example, a recent study found a map-like representation of wind direction in E-PGs, with different directions systematically represented across columns (Okubo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: The E-PG wind representation is derived from a set of ring (R1) neurons that carry wind information from the LAL.
source: This representation is derived from a set of ring (R1) neurons that carry wind information from the LAL—silencing R1 neurons abolishes most wind responses in E-PGs (Okubo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Silencing R1 neurons abolishes most wind responses in E-PGs.
source: This representation is derived from a set of ring (R1) neurons that carry wind information from the LAL—silencing R1 neurons abolishes most wind responses in E-PGs (Okubo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Other sets of ring neurons carry visual signals to E-PGs.
source: Other sets of ring neurons also carry visual signals to E-PGs (Omoto et al., 2017; Fisher et al., 2019; Turner-Evans et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In the EB, ring neurons appear to carry landmark signals of diverse modalities that collectively anchor the E-PG heading representation.
source: Thus, in the EB, ring neurons appear to carry landmark signals of diverse modalities that collectively anchor the E-PG heading representation, while P-ENs provide angular velocity signals that rotate this representation in the absence of landmark cues (Green et al., 2017; Turner-Evans et al., 2017; Turner-Evans et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: P-ENs provide angular velocity signals that rotate the E-PG heading representation in the absence of landmark cues.
source: Thus, in the EB, ring neurons appear to carry landmark signals of diverse modalities that collectively anchor the E-PG heading representation, while P-ENs provide angular velocity signals that rotate this representation in the absence of landmark cues (Green et al., 2017; Turner-Evans et al., 2017; Turner-Evans et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The model of E-PG heading representation is consistent with the fact that strong sensory responses to airflow were not observed in P-ENs.
source: This model is consistent with the fact that we did not observe strong sensory responses to airflow in P-ENs, although they are prominent in E-PGs (Okubo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the findings and prior research.

claim: Ventral P-FNs represent airflow as a set of basis vectors tuned to two orthogonal directions.
source: In contrast to the E-PG airflow 'compass', we found that ventral P-FNs represent airflow as a set of basis vectors tuned to two orthogonal directions, each originating ~45° to the left or right of the fly midline.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The airflow representation in ventral P-FNs is most likely inherited from LNa neurons.
source: Based on our imaging data, we think this representation is most likely inherited from LNa neurons, which similarly represent airflow along two orthogonal axes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from imaging data in the study.

claim: The organization of airflow information in ventral P-FNs strongly resembles that of optic flow signals in bee TN1 neurons.
source: This organization of airflow information strongly resembles that of optic flow signals in bee TN1 neurons, which similarly connect the LAL to the NO and provide input to PFN-type neurons (Stone et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Bee TN1 neurons connect the LAL to the NO and provide input to PFN-type neurons.
source: This organization of airflow information strongly resembles that of optic flow signals in bee TN1 neurons, which similarly connect the LAL to the NO and provide input to PFN-type neurons (Stone et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Two recent studies identified a basis vector representation of proprioceptive and visual self-motion cues in the two dorsal PFN cell types—P-F3N2d and P-F3N2v.
source: Two recent studies also identified a basis vector representation of proprioceptive and visual self-motion cues in the two dorsal PFN cell types—P-F3N2d and P-F3N2v, also known as PFNd and PFNv (Lu et al., 2020; Lyu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: The LAL-to-PFN system may represent flow and movement information from various modalities, organized as sets of orthogonal basis vectors.
source: Thus, the LAL-to-PFN system may represent flow and movement information from various modalities, organized as sets of orthogonal basis vectors.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study and recent research.

claim: The compass-like and basis set representations of airflow in the EB and FB are likely to arise from a common input pathway in the LAL.
source: Intriguingly, the compass-like and basis set representations of airflow in the EB and FB are likely to arise from a common input pathway in the LAL (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the findings.

claim: The branching of airflow information from the LAL may reflect the fly's need to consider sensory signals in both allocentric (compass) and egocentric (basis vector) reference frames.
source: This branching of airflow information may reflect the fly's need to consider sensory signals in both allocentric (compass) and egocentric (basis vector) reference frames.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the branching of airflow information.

claim: Electrode stimulation at many locations in the FB can produce reliable walking trajectories.
source: Martin et al., 2015 found that electrode stimulation at many locations in the FB can produce reliable walking trajectories, suggesting a fairly direct role in locomotor action selection.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Silencing of EB compass neurons (E-PGs) does not impair basic sensory orienting to a visual landmark, but only orienting at a fixed offset.
source: In contrast, silencing of EB compass neurons (E-PGs) does not impair basic sensory orienting to a visual landmark, but only orienting at a fixed offset (Giraldo et al., 2018; Green et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Different CX compartments, such as the EB and FB, support different aspects of navigation behavior.
source: These studies support a model in which different CX compartments, such as the EB and FB, support different aspects of navigation behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on prior research.

claim: Flies with silenced ventral P-FNs still turned toward the airflow source at flow off.
source: When we silenced ventral P-FNs, flies still turned toward the airflow source at flow off, suggesting that these cells are not required to detect airflow or to determine its direction.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Ventral P-FNs are not required to detect airflow or to determine its direction.
source: When we silenced ventral P-FNs, flies still turned toward the airflow source at flow off, suggesting that these cells are not required to detect airflow or to determine its direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Flies with silenced ventral P-FNs exhibited a normal range of motor behavior.
source: Flies with silenced ventral P-FNs also exhibited a normal range of motor behavior, arguing that ventral P-FNs do not generate the pool of possible responses to changing airflow direction.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments with silenced ventral P-FNs.

claim: Ventral P-FNs do not generate the pool of possible responses to changing airflow direction.
source: Flies with silenced ventral P-FNs also exhibited a normal range of motor behavior, arguing that ventral P-FNs do not generate the pool of possible responses to changing airflow direction.

source: Instead, our data suggest that ventral P-FNs guide selection from this pool, specifically converting mechanically detected changes in orientation into an appropriate turning response.

claim: The results are broadly consistent with the idea that the FB participates more directly in basic sensory orienting.
source: These results are broadly consistent with the idea that the FB participates more directly in basic sensory orienting (Honkanen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, supported by a citation to prior research.

source: A caveat is that our strongest effects were observed using a broad line (44B10-GAL4) that labels both classes of ventral P-FNs, as well as some other cells in the CX and other regions.

claim: During flight, a steady-state wind does not displace mechanoreceptors, but rather displaces the fly.
source: During flight, a steady-state wind does not displace mechanoreceptors, but rather displaces the fly (Reynolds et al., 2010; Leitch et al., 2020), generating a strong optic flow signal (Mronz and Lehmann, 2008; Theobald et al., 2010) that is often offset from a fly's heading direction.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Wind displacement of the fly generates a strong optic flow signal that is often offset from a fly's heading direction.
source: During flight, a steady-state wind does not displace mechanoreceptors, but rather displaces the fly (Reynolds et al., 2010; Leitch et al., 2020), generating a strong optic flow signal (Mronz and Lehmann, 2008; Theobald et al., 2010) that is often offset from a fly's heading direction.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Gusts or sudden changes in wind direction can transiently activate antennal mechanoreceptors in flight, leading to behavioral responses.
source: However, gusts or sudden changes in wind direction can transiently activate antennal mechanoreceptors in flight, leading to behavioral responses (Fuller et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Knowing the true direction of the wind in flight would be useful to the fly, both to control dispersal and to orient upwind toward an odor source in flight.
source: Knowing the true direction of the wind in flight would be useful to the fly, both to control dispersal (Leitch et al., 2020), and to orient upwind toward an odor source in flight (van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ventral P-FNs receive input in the protocerebral bridge (PB), presumably carrying heading information from the compass system.
source: Because ventral P-FNs receive input in the protocerebral bridge (PB), presumably carrying heading information from the compass system (Franconville et al., 2018), they may be well-poised to perform this computation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Ventral P-FNs may be well-poised to compute the true direction of the wind in flight.
source: Because ventral P-FNs receive input in the protocerebral bridge (PB), presumably carrying heading information from the compass system (Franconville et al., 2018), they may be well-poised to perform this computation.

claim: A small number of descending neurons (DNs) that participate in control of steering during flight have been identified.
source: A small number of descending neurons (DNs) that participate in control of steering during flight have been identified (Schnell et al., 2017), although a larger number of DNs target wing motor regions and presumably play a role in flight control (Namiki et al., 2018).

source: Ventral P-FNs make most of their outputs in the FB, where they synapse onto a large number of FB local neurons and FB output neurons (Scheffer et al., 2020; Hulse et al., 2020).

evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the arrangement, supported by citations to prior research.
